Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
Being emotionally close or intimate with others
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette: At 32, Alessandro's life had been hijacked by a constant sense of unease. It started two years ago when he began to notice that someone was following him home from his tutoring sessions at the local library. At first, he dismissed it as paranoia, but the feeling persisted. The stalker, later identified as an acquaintance from one of Alessandro's classes, would send him menacing messages and wait outside his apartment building. The police intervention eventually put a stop to the stalking, but not before Alessandro had become convinced that danger lurked around every corner. Even now, when someone raises their voice in conversation, Alessandro flinches, anticipating an explosion of anger. He has trouble reading people's emotions, always searching for hidden agendas. "What if they're just pretending to be calm?" he often thinks. His wife, Maria, has learned not to raise her voice, even during heated discussions. Alessandro appreciates this but feels guilty for being so on edge. Alessandro tries to stay alert by avoiding relaxation, always keeping his phone nearby and checking the locks multiple times before bed. He can't shake off the feeling that someone might be watching him, waiting for an opportunity to strike. The sound of motorcycles revving outside his window still sends a jolt through his body; it was the stalker's preferred mode of transportation. As a tutor, Alessandro used to love walking home from the library, but now he takes circuitous routes to avoid familiar places that might trigger memories of the stalking. His clients have started to notice his agitation during sessions, and some have begun to drift away. Maria has taken on more household responsibilities, trying to compensate for Alessandro's increasing withdrawal. At night, sleep eludes him as his mind replays all the what-ifs: What if he had been home when the stalker came knocking? What if Maria was in danger because of him? These thoughts lead him down a rabbit hole of self-blame and punishment thinking. "I must have done something to deserve this," he tells himself, which only fuels his anxiety. Alessandro has become increasingly distant from Maria, avoiding intimacy and physical touch. He feels unworthy of her love and is convinced that she would leave him if she knew the truth about his fears and inadequacies. Maria senses his withdrawal but doesn't know how to reach out without triggering another panic attack. One evening, as Alessandro was walking home from a tutoring session, he saw someone in the distance who looked vaguely familiar. He quickened his pace, heart racing, only to realize later that it was just a neighbor. False alarms like this have become commonplace, making him wonder if he'll ever be able to distinguish between real and perceived threats. Lately, Alessandro has started questioning whether he's cut out for teaching or even being in relationships. "What if I put someone else in danger?" he asks himself. The self-doubt is suffocating, and his mistrust of others now extends to institutions and authority figures. It was only when Maria sat him down, visibly worried about his well-being, that Alessandro realized he needed help. He's hoping therapy will teach him how to silence the cacophony in his head and learn to trust himself – and others – again.
